pickle: What is a volley in pickleball?
Hitting the ball before it bounces
What is a groundstroke?
A shot hit after the ball bounces
How wide is a standard pickleball court?
20 feet
How long is a standard pickleball court?
44 feet
How deep is the non-volley zone from the net?
7 feet
How high is the net at the center?
34 inches
How high is the net at the sidelines?
36 inches
Where does a serve start in doubles?
From the right service court at the start of a turn
Can a serve land in the kitchen?
No
What is a fault?
A rule violation that ends a rally
What does a lob do?
Sends the ball high over an opponent
What is an overhead smash?
A powerful shot hit above the head
What is a passing shot?
A shot hit beyond an opponent's reach
What is a drive?
A fast, relatively flat shot
What is a drop shot?
A soft shot that falls near the net
What is a reset shot?
A soft shot that neutralizes a hard attack
What is a speed-up?
A sudden faster attack from a slow exchange
What is a dink rally?
A series of soft kitchen shots
What is a put-away?
An attacking shot intended to end a rally
What is a third-shot drive?
A hard shot by the serving team after the return
What is stacking?
A doubles positioning tactic to favor preferred sides
What is poaching?
Crossing to intercept a partner's shot
What is an erne?
A volley hit from outside the sideline near the kitchen
What is an around-the-post shot?
A ball hit around the net post rather than over the net
Can an around-the-post shot pass below net height?
Yes, if it otherwise lands legally
Can a ball touch the net and remain in play?
Yes, if it lands legally
What is a kitchen line?
The boundary of the non-volley zone
Can you stand in the kitchen between shots?
Yes
Can you hit a ball after it bounces in the kitchen?
Yes
Can you volley with one foot touching the kitchen line?
No
Does momentum into the kitchen after a volley cause a fault?
Yes
Can your paddle cross over the kitchen during a volley?
Yes, if you do not touch the kitchen
What is the two-bounce rule?
Serve and return must each bounce before volleys
Can the serve be volleyed by the receiver?
No
Can the third shot be volleyed?
Yes, after the first two required bounces
Where must a traditional serve contact the ball?
Below waist level with an upward motion
What is a drop serve?
A serve made after dropping and bouncing the ball
Can you spin the ball with your fingers before a serve?
No, pre-spinning is prohibited
Can a traditional serve be hit overhead?
No
What is the diagonal service box?
The service court opposite the server
What does side-out scoring mean?
Only the serving team can score a point
How is a doubles score usually called?
Server score, receiver score, server number
What does the third number in doubles scoring identify?
First or second server
What does zero-zero-two mean at the start of doubles?
The opening serving team has only one server
What happens after the first server loses a rally in doubles?
The partner usually serves next
What happens after the second server loses a rally?
A side out
What happens when the serving team wins a point?
The server switches service courts
Do receivers switch courts after winning a rally?
No, not under side-out scoring
How many points usually win a game?
11, win by two
Can a game be played to 15 or 21?
Yes, depending on format
What is a match?
A contest of one or more games
What is a tournament bracket?
A chart of matchups and advancement
What is open play?
Players rotate into games with different partners
What is a round robin?
Each participant or team plays multiple others
What is a ladder league?
Players move up or down based on results
What is DUPR?
Dynamic Universal Pickleball Rating
What is the purpose of a warm-up dink?
To develop touch and control
Why keep your paddle up at the kitchen?
To react faster to quick volleys
What is a ready position?
Balanced stance with paddle in front
Why split-step?
To stabilize before reacting to a shot
Why aim deep on a return?
To keep opponents farther from the kitchen
Why follow a return toward the kitchen?
To gain a stronger net position
What is a transition zone?
The area between baseline and kitchen
What is the baseline?
The back boundary of the court
What is the centerline?
The line dividing the service courts
What is a sideline?
A side boundary of the court
Is a ball touching a boundary line usually in?
Yes, except a serve touching the kitchen line
Is a serve touching the kitchen line legal?
No
Can a player touch the net during a live rally?
No
Can you hit a ball before it crosses to your side?
Generally no, with narrow follow-through exceptions
What is a dead ball?
A ball no longer in play
What is a replay?
A rally played again under the rules
What is a distraction fault?
Deliberate action that interferes with an opponent
What is paddle face angle?
The direction the paddle surface points
What is topspin?
Forward rotation that makes a ball dip
What is backspin?
Backward rotation that can slow a bounce
What is sidespin?
Rotation that can make a ball curve sideways
What is a crosscourt dink?
A soft diagonal shot into the kitchen
What is a down-the-line shot?
A shot sent parallel to the sideline
Why target an opponent's feet?
Low balls are harder to attack
Why avoid popping up a dink?
High balls invite attacks
What is a body shot?
A ball directed toward an opponent's torso
What is a defensive block?
A compact paddle response to a hard shot
What is a soft game?
Controlled dinks, drops, and resets
What is an attackable ball?
A ball high enough for a strong shot
Why communicate in doubles?
To avoid confusion over who takes a ball
catFacts: Cats use facial scent glands to mark familiar territory.
A cat's tail position can reveal its mood.
Cats have excellent hearing for high-frequency sounds.
A cat's pupils narrow in bright light.
A cat's pupils widen in dim light.
Cats use their whiskers to sense nearby obstacles.
A cat's whiskers are deeply rooted sensory hairs.
Cats have rough tongues that help remove loose fur.
Cats often groom after meals.
Some cats groom each other as a social behavior.
Cats can learn routines and anticipate meal times.
A cat's ears can swivel toward a sound.
A cat's back legs are built for powerful jumps.
Cats use claws for climbing and gripping.
Cats retract their claws when they are not needed.
A cat's claws grow in layers.
Scratching helps cats maintain their claws.
Cats scratch to leave both visual and scent marks.
A cat's nose has many scent receptors.
Cats sometimes open their mouths after smelling something unusual.
That open-mouthed sniff is called the flehmen response.
Cats often prefer multiple small meals.
A cat's whiskers can be sensitive to the edges of deep bowls.
Cats may knead blankets before settling down.
Kneading begins as a behavior in nursing kittens.
Cats can recognize familiar people by voice and smell.
Cats may greet a person with an upright tail.
A puffed-up tail can signal fear or excitement.
Cats communicate with chirps, trills, and meows.
Adult cats often meow to communicate with people.
A cat's purr is not always a sign of happiness.
Cats can dream during sleep.
Cats have periods of rapid eye movement sleep.
Cats are most active near dawn and dusk.
A cat's eyes have a reflective layer called the tapetum lucidum.
The reflective layer helps cats see in low light.
Cats cannot see in total darkness.
Cats see motion especially well.
Cats use their tails to balance on narrow surfaces.
Cats have flexible shoulder joints.
Cats have a relatively flexible spine.
A cat's collarbones are small and loosely connected.
Cats usually land on their feet using a righting reflex.
A righting reflex does not make falls safe.
Cats may seek high places to feel secure.
Cats enjoy exploring new scents.
A cardboard box can provide a hiding place for a cat.
Cats often prefer predictable routines.
Cats may rub against furniture to leave familiar scents.
Cats have scent glands between their toes.
A cat's paw pads help absorb landing impacts.
Cats can sweat through their paw pads.
Cats have five toes on most front paws.
Cats usually have four toes on each back paw.
Some cats have extra toes, a trait called polydactyly.
A group of kittens is called a litter.
A female cat is sometimes called a queen.
A male breeding cat is sometimes called a tom.
A kitten's baby teeth are replaced as it grows.
Cats are obligate carnivores.
Cats need nutrients found naturally in animal tissues.
A cat's tongue has tiny hooks called papillae.
Those papillae help cats groom their coats.
Cats may chatter while watching birds through a window.
A catio lets cats enjoy outdoor sights in an enclosure.
Indoor cats benefit from climbing and scratching opportunities.
Cats can learn tricks with reward-based training.
Cats may play with toys that mimic prey movements.
Short play sessions can match a cat's natural hunting style.
